newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory cocoa arrivals on target, beans export size.
newsitem.headline: Ivory cocoa arrivals on target, beans export size.

text.p: Declared arrivals of Ivory Coast's cocoa crop to end-September are between 1.19 million and 1.2 million tonnes, in line with forecasts, exporters said.
Arriving mid-crop beans were close to main-crop average sizes at 95 to 115 beans per 100 grammes, against 130 per 100 grammes a year ago, they added.

"Humidity is about eight or nine percent so beans have to be dried at the factories. Drying has delayed arrivals but beans are export size," said a purchasing manager for a large exporter with sites throughout Ivory Coast.
He said weekly arrivals could be above 3,000 tonnes per week. Some sources put the total at 4,500 tonnes.

Unrest in the run-up to presidential elections last October disrupted arrivals so figures were not representative. End of year arrival estimates -- October 6 in 1995 -- were 892,000 tonnes, against 888,000 in 1993/94.
A crop analyst recently back from an up-country trip said some buyers were stocking in anticipation of a small farm-gate price rise at the start of the 96/97 main crop season.

"I have seen some stocks in warehouses. Mid-crop beans are now main crop size so it will be easy to mix them together. Farm prices are higher in Ghana and I think political pressure will override any freezing of the price here," he said.
Carry-over of mid-crop to the main crop in Ivory Coast was typically in the 40-70,000 tonne range, he added.
One buyer in San Pedro said factories offered undiscounted prices for beans as mid-crop quality was good, and were taking delivery or going to collect from sellers.
"Nothing is being held at farm level. If anyone is storing it will be factories. They have the silos," said another.
A large exporter said central and centre-west harvests were above average, particularly around Gagnoa, Soubre and San Pedro.
Exporters in Gagnoa and Daloa said bean sizes were 95-100 per 100 grammes while an Abidjan-based exporter said beans were still around 110-115 against 130 at the same time last year.
July rains were reported to be the heaviest in 20 years.
"Even August had about about twice the usual rainfall. But September...has been much drier than usual, on average 50 percent less in the first 26 days," said a weather analyst.
From September 1-20 Man and Daloa in the north had heavier rains while Gagnoa and Abidjan were among the driest areas. But San Pedro had more rain in the past 10 days than earlier.
"We still need a bit more sun before the 1996/97 season," said a crop analyst. He added it was too early to predict the effect of the weather on the eventual main crop harvest in 1997.
Buyers say arriving cocoa bean sack quality has fallen and a lot of new ones will be needed in 1996/97.
"New sacks cost about 500 CFA, a good second-hand one about 300. Exporters will probably supply better ones to buyers next season," said Daloa-based buyer Makkram Haddad.
Farmers at a review of the 1995/96 season in Abidjan last week complained bagged cocoa buyers returned sacks too late.

"Sometimes it takes two weeks for sacks to be returned. Often they are someone else's and in poorer condition," said one SYNAGCI farm union offical. The 1995/96 bagged cocoa farm-gate price of 320 CFA per kilo includes five CFAs for the sack.
"The rate should be more like 15 CFA," said one buyer.
As the 1995/96 season closes some buyers expect a smaller main crop next year than crop forecaster estimates of 850,000-930,000 tonnes, 20 percent down on this year's record.
"The trees are tired. I would say less," said Haddad.

Exporters were less conservative. "There are plenty of pods on the trees. We should see around 900,000 to one million tonnes," one said. "We expect a November, December, January peak but October will be a little weak."

Agriculture Minister Lambert Kouassi Konan has set October 15 as the start of the 1996/97 season and commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze told Reuters last week the cocoa farmgate price for the year would also be set around then. --Abidjan newsroom +225 21 90 90
